svg.title: A bundle losing members one at a time: bandwidth falls silently until min-links converts the degradation into a deliberate outage
svg.desc: A bar chart of aggregate bandwidth as members fail. With eight members the bundle gives eighty gigabits, seven gives seventy, six sixty and five fifty, all shown in red because the bundle is still up while the design assumption is already broken. At four members the bundle reaches min-links, drawn as a boundary, and below four the port channel goes down entirely and traffic follows the backup path. A box on the right lists the availability details: members spread across line cards, optics from the same batch, min-links set to the bandwidth you can accept, fast LACP rate, and the rehashing that follows every member change.
svg.text: A bundle does not fail. It gets quieter, which is harder to notice and harder to explain
Every member lost is bandwidth gone with all links still green in the monitoring tool
Gb/s
down
down
down
MEMBERS STILL UP
min-links 4
bundle goes down, traffic follows the backup path
still up, already below the design assumption
AVAILABILITY DETAILS THAT DECIDE THE OUTCOME
Members across line cards
One card failure should cost one member, not the bundle.
Optics from the same batch
Not enforced by any protocol; a bad batch still fails as a batch.
min-links at the accepted minimum
Turn silent degradation into one deliberate, visible event.
Fast LACP rate
Faster member failure detection, at the cost of more chatter.
Rehashing on every change
A member leaving reorders flows; expect a brief spike, not an outage.
The dangerous window is the red part of the chart: eight members down to five still shows a healthy bundle in every dashboard, at half the bandwidth the design assumed.
min-links does not add bandwidth. It converts a long quiet degradation into one event with an alarm, which is all operations can act on.
Set it to the bandwidth the application really needs, not to the number that lets the bundle stay up.
Chapter rule: every bundle gets min-links, a member spread across cards, and an alarm on the member count.
Three settings, one minute each, and the difference between a designed failure and an unexplained slowdown six months later.
